cards.q: In what environment do spores of fungi occur?
cards.a:
**In hot and humid, or arid, tropical environments.**

## Understanding it
- Fungi thrive where it is warm — both humid and dry tropical settings.

>> Warm tropical environments (humid or arid).
opts: Hot and humid, or arid, tropical environments

cards.q: What factors favour the spread of fungal infections among children?
cards.a:
**Poor personal/community hygiene; closeness among large families; and institutions (e.g. schools, orphanages).**

## Understanding it
- Crowding, close contact and poor hygiene spread the spores.

>> Poor hygiene, crowding, institutions.
opts: Poor hygiene, crowding in large families, institutions

cards.q: Which body structures do most fungal infections affect?
cards.a:
**The skin, hair, nails and mucosa.**

## Understanding it
- Superficial fungi favour **keratinised** tissues (skin, hair, nails) and mucosa.

>> Skin, hair, nails, mucosa.

cards.q: List the five superficial fungal skin infections.
cards.a:
**Candidiasis, tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, and pityriasis versicolor.**

## Understanding it
- Superficial = candida + the tineas + pityriasis versicolor (stratum corneum/keratin).

>> Candidiasis, tinea capitis/corporis/pedis, pityriasis versicolor.
opts: Candidiasis, tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, pityriasis versicolor

cards.q: List the five deep fungal skin infections.
cards.a:
**Mycetoma (Madura foot), blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, and sporotrichosis.**

## Understanding it
- Deep mycoses invade subcutaneous tissue/organs (often after inhalation or implantation).

>> Mycetoma, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis, sporotrichosis.

cards.q: Which organisms cause candidiasis?
cards.a:
**Candida albicans (and C. tropicalis, C. stellatoidea, C. krusei) — yeasts of the genus Candida.**

## Understanding it
- Candidiasis is caused by yeasts, chiefly **C. albicans**.

>> Candida species (mainly C. albicans).

cards.q: Where do candida infections usually occur?
cards.a:
**On the skin, mucous membranes, nail folds and nails, GI tract and genital tract.**

## Understanding it
- Candida favours warm, moist surfaces — mucosa, skin folds, nails, gut, genitals.

>> Skin, mucosa, nails, GI and genital tract.
opts: Skin, mucosa, nail folds, GI and genital tract

cards.q: Describe the skin lesions of candidiasis and where they occur.
cards.a:
**Dusky red, macerated or erosive lesions in skin folds (neck, flanks, large flexures) — moist, intertriginous areas.**

## Understanding it
- Candida loves warm moist **flexures/folds** → red macerated intertrigo, often with satellite lesions.

>> Red macerated lesions in moist skin folds.
opts: Scaly annular plaques on dry skin
Dusky red, macerated lesions in moist skin folds

cards.q: What may follow scratching of candidal skin lesions?
cards.a:
**Fissuring and bleeding, with secondary bacterial infection.**

## Understanding it
- Scratching breaks the macerated skin → fissures, bleeding and secondary bacterial infection.

>> Fissuring, bleeding, secondary bacterial infection.
opts: Fissuring, bleeding and secondary bacterial infection

cards.q: Which organism most commonly causes oral thrush?
cards.a:
**Candida albicans.**

## Understanding it
- Oral thrush is almost always **C. albicans**.

>> Oral thrush = C. albicans.

cards.q: Describe the lesions of oral candidiasis.
cards.a:
**Curdy or whitish-grey, friable, cheesy pseudomembranous patches/plaques on markedly red mucosa.**

## Understanding it
- White 'cheesy' plaques on inflamed mucosa that **rub off** (unlike leukoplakia).

>> White cheesy pseudomembranous plaques on red mucosa.
opts: White cheesy pseudomembranous plaques on red mucosa

cards.q: Where may the plaques of thrush be found?
cards.a:
**On the lips, buccal mucosa, tongue and palate, extending to the pharynx/oesophagus (the tract lining is continuous).**

## Understanding it
- Thrush can spread along the continuous mucosa into the oesophagus/pharynx.

>> Lips, cheeks, tongue, palate — may reach the oesophagus.
opts: Only the soles of the feet
Lips, buccal mucosa, tongue, palate — may extend to the oesophagus

cards.q: What happens on removal of the plaques of thrush, and why is this useful?
cards.a:
**Removal may cause mild punctate bleeding, which helps confirm the diagnosis.**

## Understanding it
- Scraping thrush leaves a raw, **pinpoint-bleeding** base — a useful bedside clue (unlike leukoplakia).

>> Plaques rub off leaving pinpoint bleeding (diagnostic clue).
opts: They rub off, leaving punctate bleeding (a diagnostic clue)
They cannot be removed at all

cards.q: List the factors predisposing to candidiasis.
cards.a:
**Diabetes mellitus, retroviral disease (HIV), prolonged antibiotic and corticosteroid use, and immunosuppression.**

## Understanding it
- Candida overgrows when **immunity is low** or **normal flora is wiped out** (antibiotics).

>> Diabetes, HIV, antibiotics/steroids, immunosuppression.

cards.q: Give the treatment of oral candidiasis.
cards.a:
**Topical antifungals (clotrimazole, nystatin, amphotericin B, or miconazole gel), plus treating any predisposing factor.**

## Understanding it
- Local antifungals for thrush, and fix the underlying cause (e.g. control diabetes, review antibiotics/steroids).

>> Nystatin/clotrimazole/miconazole + treat the cause.

cards.q: What is tinea capitis and which organism most often causes it?
cards.a:
**A dermatophyte infection of the scalp, most often caused by Trichophyton tonsurans.**

## Understanding it
- Tinea capitis = scalp ringworm, usually **T. tonsurans**.

>> Scalp dermatophytosis; usually T. tonsurans.
opts: Scalp dermatophyte infection — usually T. tonsurans
A candida infection of the scalp

cards.q: Describe the lesions and hairs in tinea capitis.
cards.a:
**Erythematous, scaly, circular (ring) plaques within which the infected hairs break off.**

## Understanding it
- Ringworm plaques on the scalp with **broken hairs** (leaving black dots/stubble).

>> Scaly ring plaques with broken-off hairs.
opts: Scaly circular plaques with broken-off hairs
White cheesy plaques that rub off

cards.q: What appearance do multiple affected sites produce in tinea capitis?
cards.a:
**A moth-eaten appearance of the hair.**

## Understanding it
- Multiple patches of broken hair give a patchy 'moth-eaten' look.

>> Moth-eaten hair appearance.
opts: A moth-eaten appearance of the hair

cards.q: What else may develop in tinea capitis?
cards.a:
**Numerous confluent patches of alopecia, with variable scaling and scalp inflammation.**

## Understanding it
- Hair loss (alopecia) plus scaling/inflammation of variable severity.

>> Patchy alopecia with scaling/inflammation.
opts: Confluent patches of alopecia with scaling/inflammation

cards.q: What is a kerion and what causes it?
cards.a:
**An inflammatory, boggy, pus-covered mass — a severe hypersensitivity/inflammatory reaction to the scalp dermatophyte.**

## Understanding it
- A kerion is an intense **inflammatory** response to tinea capitis; it can scar if untreated.

>> Kerion = boggy inflamed pustular scalp mass (severe tinea reaction).
opts: A boggy, inflamed, pustular scalp mass (severe tinea reaction)

cards.q: What is favus and which organism causes it?
cards.a:
**A severe, chronic form of tinea capitis, typically caused by Trichophyton schoenleinii.**

## Understanding it
- Favus is chronic scalp tinea (T. schoenleinii) forming cup-shaped crusts (scutula).

>> Favus = chronic tinea capitis (T. schoenleinii).
opts: Chronic tinea capitis caused by T. schoenleinii

cards.q: Describe the lesions of favus.
cards.a:
**Thick, yellowish, cup-shaped crusts (scutula) that develop around hair follicles.**

## Understanding it
- The hallmark is **scutula** — yellow cup-shaped crusts around follicles.

>> Yellow cup-shaped scutula around follicles.

cards.q: What happens if favus is left untreated?
cards.a:
**It destroys hair follicles, mats the hair, and causes permanent scarring alopecia.**

## Understanding it
- Untreated favus scars the scalp → **permanent (scarring) hair loss**.

>> Untreated favus → permanent scarring alopecia.
opts: Follicle destruction, matting, and permanent scarring alopecia

cards.q: How is tinea capitis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
**Diagnosis by scraping + KOH microscopy (± Wood lamp/culture); treatment needs ORAL antifungals (griseofulvin, itraconazole or terbinafine).**

## Understanding it
- Because the fungus is **inside the hair shaft**, topical treatment can't reach it — **oral** antifungals are required.

>> KOH scraping; ORAL griseofulvin/itraconazole/terbinafine.

cards.q: Define tinea corporis.
cards.a:
**A fungal (dermatophyte) infection of the glabrous (hairless) skin, excluding palms, soles and groin.**

## Understanding it
- Tinea corporis = ringworm of the **body skin** (not palms/soles/groin, which have their own names).

>> Ringworm of glabrous body skin (not palms/soles/groin).
opts: Dermatophyte infection of glabrous body skin

cards.q: Which organisms most commonly cause tinea corporis?
cards.a:
**Trichophyton rubrum and T. mentagrophytes (also Microsporum canis and Epidermophyton).**

## Understanding it
- Dermatophytes — chiefly **T. rubrum/mentagrophytes**; M. canis comes from pets.

>> T. rubrum/mentagrophytes (M. canis from pets).

cards.q: Describe the characteristic lesion of tinea corporis.
cards.a:
**A dry, mildly erythematous, elevated, scaly papule/plaque that spreads centrifugally with central clearing (an active advancing edge).**

## Understanding it
- The classic **annular ('ring') lesion** — active scaly border, clearing centre.

>> Annular plaque: active scaly edge, central clearing.
opts: Annular scaly plaque with an active edge and central clearing

cards.q: How is tinea corporis acquired?
cards.a:
**By direct contact from an infected person, contaminated surfaces, or pets (M. canis).**

## Understanding it
- Spread by contact — people, fomites, and animals (kittens/puppies for M. canis).

>> Contact with infected people, surfaces, or pets.
opts: Direct contact with infected people, surfaces or pets

cards.q: Name the forms of tinea corporis according to site.
cards.a:
**Tinea faciale (face), tinea axillaris (axilla), tinea cruris (groin), tinea manuum (hand), etc. — named by body region.**

## Understanding it
- The same infection is named by **site** (faciale, cruris, manuum, pedis, capitis).

>> Named by region: faciale, cruris, manuum, etc.
opts: Named by body region (faciale, cruris, manuum, etc.)

cards.q: How is tinea corporis diagnosed?
cards.a:
**Clinically; by skin scraping + KOH microscopy; and by culture of scrapings for identification.**

## Understanding it
- KOH microscopy of the **advancing scaly edge** shows hyphae; culture identifies the species.

>> Clinical + KOH scraping (± culture).
opts: Clinically and by KOH microscopy of scrapings (± culture)

cards.q: Give the treatment of tinea corporis.
cards.a:
**Topical antifungals (imidazoles, terbinafine or naftifine); oral antifungals in severe/extensive cases.**

## Understanding it
- Localised disease → **topical** antifungal; widespread → oral.

>> Topical antifungal (oral if severe).

cards.q: What is tinea pedis and which organisms cause it?
cards.a:
**Athlete's foot — infection of the toe webs and soles, caused by Trichophyton (rubrum/mentagrophytes) and Epidermophyton.**

## Understanding it
- Tinea pedis = foot dermatophytosis (toe webs/soles), classic dermatophytes.

>> Athlete's foot; Trichophyton/Epidermophyton.
opts: A candida infection of the feet

cards.q: Describe the usual appearance of tinea pedis.
cards.a:
**The subdigital (toe-web) crevices are fissured, with maceration and peeling of the surrounding skin.**

## Understanding it
- Classic interdigital tinea pedis: **macerated, fissured, peeling toe webs** (esp. 4th web).

>> Macerated, fissured, peeling toe webs.

cards.q: Describe the less common presentations of tinea pedis.
cards.a:
**A chronic diffuse hyperkeratosis of the sole ('moccasin' pattern) with only slight erythema.**

## Understanding it
- Besides toe-web disease, tinea pedis can cause a dry **scaly thickening of the whole sole** (moccasin type).

>> Chronic hyperkeratotic 'moccasin' sole.
opts: Chronic diffuse hyperkeratosis of the sole (moccasin type)

cards.q: Which symptoms are characteristic of tinea pedis?
cards.a:
**Severe tenderness, itching, and a persistent foul odour.**

## Understanding it
- Itch, tenderness and a characteristic **foul smell** of the feet.

>> Itching, tenderness, foul odour.

cards.q: How is tinea pedis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
**Diagnosis by fungal hyphae on KOH microscopy (± culture); treatment with topical antifungals (and keeping the feet dry), oral antifungals if severe.**

## Understanding it
- KOH shows hyphae; treat with topical antifungal + moisture control; oral for resistant/severe.

>> KOH; topical antifungal + dry feet (oral if severe).
opts: KOH microscopy; topical antifungals and keeping feet dry

cards.q: What is pityriasis versicolor and which organism causes it?
cards.a:
**A common chronic infection of the stratum corneum caused by the dimorphic yeast Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum).**

## Understanding it
- Not a dermatophyte — caused by **Malassezia**, a lipophilic skin yeast.

>> Malassezia furfur infection of the stratum corneum.
opts: Malassezia furfur infection of the stratum corneum

cards.q: In whom is pityriasis versicolor most prevalent?
cards.a:
**Adolescents and young adults.**

## Understanding it
- It peaks in **adolescents/young adults** (active sebaceous glands feed the lipophilic yeast).

>> Adolescents and young adults.

cards.q: List the predisposing factors to pityriasis versicolor.
cards.a:
**A warm humid environment, excessive sweating, occlusion, high plasma cortisol, and immunosuppression.**

## Understanding it
- Heat, sweat, occlusion and high cortisol/immunosuppression favour Malassezia overgrowth.

>> Heat, sweating, occlusion, high cortisol, immunosuppression.
opts: Cold dry climate and good hygiene
Warm humid climate, sweating, occlusion, high cortisol, immunosuppression

cards.q: Describe the lesions of pityriasis versicolor and their sites.
cards.a:
**Hypo- or hyperpigmented macules with a fine scale, often merging into patches, mainly on the trunk, neck and upper arms.**

## Understanding it
- Variably-coloured ('versicolor') finely-scaly macules on the **upper trunk**.

>> Hypo/hyperpigmented finely-scaly macules on the trunk.
opts: Hypo/hyperpigmented finely-scaly macules on the trunk

cards.q: How is pityriasis versicolor diagnosed?
cards.a:
**Wood lamp (yellow fluorescence), KOH preparation of scrapings ('spaghetti and meatballs'), and skin biopsy.**

## Understanding it
- KOH shows the classic **short hyphae + spores** ('spaghetti and meatballs'); Wood lamp fluoresces.

>> Wood lamp + KOH ('spaghetti and meatballs').
opts: Wood lamp, KOH scrapings, and biopsy

cards.q: Give the treatment of pityriasis versicolor.
cards.a:
**Selenium sulfide suspension overnight; imidazole or terbinafine cream twice daily; oral antifungals for extensive disease.**

## Understanding it
- Topical selenium sulfide/azoles; oral azoles if widespread. (Repigmentation lags after cure.)

>> Selenium sulfide/azole cream (oral if extensive).
opts: Selenium sulfide and azole/terbinafine creams (oral if extensive)

cards.q: What causes histoplasmosis and how is it acquired?
cards.a:
**Histoplasma capsulatum and H. duboisii — dimorphic fungi acquired by inhaling fungal spores.**

## Understanding it
- A **deep mycosis** acquired by **inhalation** (not skin contact).

>> Histoplasma; inhaled spores.

cards.q: Where are the fungi of histoplasmosis found?
cards.a:
**In soil and in the droppings of some animals — e.g. bats and poultry.**

## Understanding it
- Histoplasma grows in soil enriched with **bat/bird droppings**.

>> Soil with bat/bird droppings.

cards.q: Describe the spread of histoplasmosis.
cards.a:
**Primary infection is in the lungs, with haematogenous spread to the liver, bone marrow, spleen and other organs.**

## Understanding it
- Starts in the **lungs**, then disseminates via the blood to reticuloendothelial organs.

>> Lungs first, then blood-borne spread to organs.
opts: Lungs first, then haematogenous spread to organs

cards.q: How does African histoplasmosis (H. duboisii) present?
cards.a:
**As subcutaneous nodules that tend to umbilicate and suppurate or ulcerate as they grow.**

## Understanding it
- H. duboisii (African) is more **cutaneous/subcutaneous and bony** than pulmonary.

>> Subcutaneous nodules that umbilicate/ulcerate.
opts: Subcutaneous nodules that umbilicate and ulcerate

cards.q: How does H. capsulatum characteristically present?
cards.a:
**It affects the lungs, presenting with productive cough and constitutional symptoms.**

## Understanding it
- Classic H. capsulatum is a **pulmonary** illness (cough + constitutional symptoms).

>> Pulmonary — cough and constitutional symptoms.
opts: Pulmonary — productive cough and constitutional symptoms

cards.q: How is histoplasmosis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
**By isolating/identifying the fungus in cultures (sputum, bone marrow, etc.); treated with antifungals such as amphotericin B or itraconazole.**

## Understanding it
- Culture/identification confirms it; treat with **amphotericin B/itraconazole**.

>> Culture; amphotericin B/itraconazole.

cards.q: What causes sporotrichosis and how is it acquired?
cards.a:
**Accidental implantation into the skin of Sporothrix schenckii, which grows on thorny plants/vegetation.**

## Understanding it
- The 'rose-gardener's disease' — **implanted** by a thorn prick, not inhaled.

>> Sporothrix schenckii, implanted by thorns.
opts: Sporothrix schenckii, implanted through skin trauma (thorns)

cards.q: Describe the initial lesion of sporotrichosis.
cards.a:
**A firm, painless or mildly tender subcutaneous nodule at the site of skin trauma.**

## Understanding it
- Starts as a solitary **subcutaneous nodule** at the inoculation site.

>> Painless subcutaneous nodule at the trauma site.
opts: A painless/mildly tender subcutaneous nodule at the injury site

cards.q: How does the sporotrichosis nodule progress?
cards.a:
**The primary nodule enlarges, becomes pustular, and may open into a chronic ulcer, with new nodules tracking along lymphatics.**

## Understanding it
- Classic **lymphocutaneous** spread — a chain of nodules/ulcers along the draining lymphatics.

>> Ulcerates and spreads along lymphatics (nodular chain).
opts: Spreads by inhalation to the lungs
Ulcerates and spreads along lymphatics as a nodular chain

cards.q: How may sporotrichosis spread?
cards.a:
**By lymphatic or haematogenous routes to muscles, bones, joints or other tissues (inhalation can cause pulmonary disease).**

## Understanding it
- Mostly lymphocutaneous, but can disseminate to bone/joint or (rarely, if inhaled) the lungs.

>> Lymphatic/haematogenous spread (± pulmonary if inhaled).
opts: It never spreads beyond the skin
Lymphatic/haematogenous spread to bone, joints, etc.

cards.q: How is sporotrichosis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
**Diagnosis by microscopy/culture of the fungus from scrapings or biopsy; treated with itraconazole (or potassium iodide; amphotericin B for severe/systemic).**

## Understanding it
- Culture confirms; **itraconazole** is standard (KI historically; amphotericin for systemic).

>> Culture; itraconazole (± KI / amphotericin B).

cards.q: What causes blastomycosis and how is it acquired?
cards.a:
**Blastomyces dermatitidis, acquired by inhaling fungal spores.**

## Understanding it
- A deep mycosis acquired by **inhalation** (lungs first).

>> Blastomyces dermatitidis; inhaled.

cards.q: Describe the spread and skin lesions of blastomycosis.
cards.a:
**Primary lung infection with haematogenous spread to skin, bone and genitalia; skin lesions are verrucous/ulcerated.**

## Understanding it
- Lungs → blood → **skin (warty/ulcerated), bone, GU tract**.

>> Lungs first; then skin (verrucous), bone, GU.
opts: Lungs first, then skin (verrucous/ulcerated), bone and GU

cards.q: How is blastomycosis diagnosed and treated?
cards.a:
**Diagnosis by characteristic broad-based budding yeast on KOH of specimens (± culture); treated with amphotericin B or itraconazole.**

## Understanding it
- Broad-based **budding yeast** on microscopy; treat with amphotericin B/itraconazole.

>> Broad-based budding yeast; amphotericin B/itraconazole.
opts: Broad-based budding yeast on KOH; amphotericin B/itraconazole

cards.q: What causes coccidiomycosis and how does it spread?
cards.a:
**Coccidioides immitis, a dimorphic fungus acquired by inhaling spores; primary infection is pulmonary with possible dissemination.**

## Understanding it
- Inhaled Coccidioides → **lung** infection that may disseminate.

>> Coccidioides immitis, inhaled; pulmonary then disseminates.
opts: Coccidioides immitis, inhaled; pulmonary then may disseminate

cards.q: What do the skin lesions of coccidiomycosis consist of, and how is it treated?
cards.a:
**Panniculitis, abscesses and draining sinuses; treated with oral ketoconazole or itraconazole (amphotericin B for severe disease).**

## Understanding it
- Cutaneous coccidioidomycosis: **panniculitis/abscesses/sinuses**; azoles (± amphotericin).

>> Panniculitis/abscesses/sinuses; ketoconazole/itraconazole.

cards.q: What is mycetoma and which structures does it affect?
cards.a:
**Madura foot — a chronic infection of the skin, subcutaneous tissue and bones of the feet.**

## Understanding it
- Mycetoma ('Madura foot') chronically destroys the **skin, subcutis and bone** of the foot.

>> Chronic skin/subcutaneous/bone infection of the foot.
opts: Chronic infection of skin, subcutaneous tissue and bone of the foot

cards.q: How does mycetoma develop, and in whom is it common?
cards.a:
**It develops very slowly and is rare in children; organisms are implanted through the skin (typically in adults doing barefoot outdoor work).**

## Understanding it
- A slow, chronic implantation infection — **rare in children**, common in barefoot rural adults.

>> Slow-developing; rare in children (implanted through skin).
opts: Very slow-developing; rare in children (skin implantation)

cards.q: Distinguish eumycetoma from actinomycetoma.
cards.a:
**Eumycetoma is caused by true fungi; actinomycetoma is caused by filamentous bacteria (actinomycetes).**

## Understanding it
- Same clinical picture, two causes: **fungi (eu-)** vs **bacteria (actino-)** — which matters for treatment.

>> Eumycetoma = fungi; actinomycetoma = filamentous bacteria.

cards.q: Name the causative organisms of mycetoma.
cards.a:
**Actinomycetes such as Nocardia brasiliensis, Actinomadura madurae and Streptomyces somaliensis (plus true fungi in eumycetoma).**

## Understanding it
- Actinomycetoma organisms: **Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces**; eumycetoma is true fungi.

>> Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces (± true fungi).
opts: Nocardia, Actinomadura, Streptomyces (and true fungi in eumycetoma)

cards.q: What is the treatment of mycetoma?
cards.a:
**Itraconazole (with prolonged therapy; actinomycetoma also needs antibacterials such as co-trimoxazole).**

## Understanding it
- Prolonged antifungal (itraconazole) for eumycetoma; actinomycetoma additionally needs antibacterials.

>> Itraconazole (prolonged; antibacterials for actinomycetoma).
